identification.title: God the Uncreated One (King Forevermore)
identification.notes: Words and music by Aaron Keyes and Pete James. CCLI 7057478. Copyright 2016 to 10000 Fathers, Common Hymnal Publishing, Thankyou Music and Getty Music Hymns and Songs. Credited to Aaron Keyes as the artist whose recording carried it into congregational use.

claims.structuralNotes: Four strophic verses, each closing on the same refrain shape with one word changed at the front ('He is King forever…', 'Crown him King forever…', 'Reign as King forever…'), resolving on 'King of Kings forevermore'. The verses run in sequence: creation, God's rule over history, the incarnation and cross, eternal reign.

claims.claim: God is uncreated — the source of everything, deriving his being from nothing outside himself.
claims.subject: Aseity

claims.claim: God spoke creation into being, and his attention runs from the stars to the smallest particulars.
claims.subject: Creation

claims.claim: The God who orders the cosmos also knows each person inwardly.
claims.subject: Omniscience
claims.lyricExcerpt: knows the heart of every man

claims.claim: God is the refuge and strength of his people.
claims.subject: Providence

claims.claim: God does not change; he is the same self-existent God who named himself to Moses.
claims.subject: Immutability

claims.claim: Empires rise and collapse without affecting God's faithfulness.
claims.subject: Providence over history

claims.claim: The same almighty God took on real, mortal human nature.
claims.subject: Incarnation

claims.claim: Christ died as a flawless sacrifice offered on behalf of others.
claims.subject: Substitutionary atonement

claims.claim: Christ was raised — the Father delivered him from death.
claims.subject: Resurrection

claims.claim: Christ is to be crowned as king, and his reign has no end.
claims.subject: Kingship of Christ
claims.lyricExcerpt: He is King forever, He is King forevermore

claims.claim: The life God gives is everlasting and his rule is just.
claims.subject: Eternal life and justice

theological.assessment: Unusually substantial for a contemporary song: aseity, creation, providence, immutability, incarnation, substitution, resurrection and reign, all orthodox and none muddled. Its limits are scope rather than accuracy — sin is assumed and the Spirit is absent.

strengths.title: Opens on aseity
strengths.explanation: It asserts God is uncreated — the source of everything, dependent on nothing. Congregational song almost never attempts this, and rarely without muddling it.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: The God who made the world and everything in it… is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Paul's argument in Athens is the hymn's opening claim exactly.

strengths.title: The whole gospel arc, in order
strengths.explanation: Incarnation, cross, resurrection, reign — in sequence, with no stage collapsed into another. Many songs that reach the cross never reach the resurrection.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death… Therefore God has highly exalted him.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Paul's hymn runs the same course and ends, as this one does, on kingship.

strengths.title: The one who dies is the one who was never made
strengths.explanation: The hymn does not change subject at the incarnation. That continuity is a demanding claim about who Jesus is, and it is made structurally rather than merely asserted.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.
strengths.scriptureRationale: John makes the same identification of the eternal Word with the man.

strengths.title: Substitution stated plainly
strengths.explanation: A spotless sacrifice offered for us — not merely an example of love. That is the specific claim which makes the cross good news rather than only moving.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: Ransomed… with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Peter supplies the exact sacrificial register the hymn borrows.

strengths.title: Immutability made pastoral
strengths.explanation: Kingdoms rise and fall; God does not. The comfort offered is that God will hold, not that circumstances will — a far more durable consolation.
strengths.lyricExcerpt: he is faithful through it all
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Political instability as an instance of God's rule, not evidence against it.

strengths.title: Transcendence and immanence in one breath
strengths.explanation: The first verse moves from the scale of the heavens to the count of the sand to the inside of a person, as one continuous thought rather than two competing ideas.
strengths.lyricExcerpt: knows the heart of every man
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The psalm makes the identical move from cosmic scale to personal attention.

concerns.title: Sin is assumed, never named
concerns.explanation: The sacrifice is stated but what it addresses is not, so a congregation can sing all four verses without facing its own guilt. Pair it with a song of confession.
concerns.scriptureExcerpt: All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift.
concerns.scriptureRationale: Paul will not state the remedy without first stating the condition.

concerns.title: The Spirit does not appear
concerns.explanation: Four verses survey God's nature and works without the hymn ever becoming Trinitarian. A planning observation rather than a fault in the text.
concerns.scriptureExcerpt: Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
concerns.scriptureRationale: A diet of such songs leaves a congregation without the threefold name.

concerns.title: Clothing imagery is imprecise if pressed
concerns.explanation: Putting flesh on can suggest humanity worn rather than genuinely assumed. The hymn's own mortality and death language rules that reading out, and Wesley used the same idiom.
concerns.scriptureExcerpt: He himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death.
concerns.scriptureRationale: Only a genuinely human death accomplishes anything.

communal.assessment: Built for a congregation: strophic, one repeated refrain shape, declarative voice. Length invites cutting. The vocal range was not independently verified — published in E and F, so check the tessitura locally before introducing it.
communal.vocalRangeNote: Not verified. Published arrangements appear in E and F; check locally and transpose without hesitation.
communal.repetitionAssessment: What repeats is 'forever' — the claim the hymn exists to make. Meaningful repetition, not padding.

strengths.title: One refrain, learned once
strengths.explanation: Only the opening word changes between verses, so a congregation effectively learns one refrain and can join in from the first verse.

strengths.title: Declarative, not confessional-personal
strengths.explanation: It tells the truth about God rather than reporting private experience, so there is no feeling a singer must borrow in order to mean the words.

strengths.title: The repeated word is the doctrine
strengths.explanation: 'Forever' is the claim, not filler, and it lets a congregation sing each verse's close without looking at a page.

concerns.title: Four verses invite cutting the best one
concerns.explanation: The verse most likely dropped for time is the third — incarnation, cross, resurrection — which is the one the hymn least survives without.

clarity.assessment: Clear despite the doctrinal density: concrete biblical imagery, contemporary diction, almost no archaism. Two small frictions worth a sentence of introduction the first time a congregation meets it.

strengths.title: Biblical pictures, not abstraction
strengths.explanation: Stars, sand, fortress, rock — Scripture's own images for these attributes, so hard doctrine arrives already graspable.
strengths.scriptureExcerpt: The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The images arrive carrying their biblical sense already.

strengths.title: One line carries two doctrines
strengths.explanation: Kingdoms rising and falling set against God's faithfulness puts providence and immutability into a phrase people take home.

strengths.title: Hymn weight without archaism
strengths.explanation: Traditional structure and contemporary vocabulary — almost nothing a first-time visitor would need translated.

concerns.title: 'Uncreated' needs a sentence of introduction
concerns.explanation: The word does real theological work but is not everyday speech; some will sing it without registering the claim.

concerns.title: The referent shifts unannounced
concerns.explanation: 'He' becomes the crucified Christ mid-hymn while the Father appears as a distinct actor. Theologically the continuity is the point, but it is momentarily demanding.
concerns.scriptureExcerpt: He is the image of the invisible God… by him all things were created… and in him all things hold together.
concerns.scriptureRationale: Paul makes the same identification, which is why the shift is defensible.

synthesis.summary: A doctrinally dense modern hymn that runs from God's self-existence through creation, providence, the incarnation, a plainly substitutionary cross and Christ's unending reign — never changing subject along the way. Sin is assumed rather than named, so it sits best alongside a song of confession. Weighty content, unusually easy to sing.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: The God who made the world and everything in it… is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The opening doctrine: God as source of all, dependent on none.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: Before the mountains were brought forth… from everlasting to everlasting you are God.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The eternality behind calling God uncreated.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names.
scriptureReferences.relevance: Verse one's move from cosmic scale to personal knowledge.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: For I the LORD do not change.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The immutability verse two rests its comfort on.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings.
scriptureReferences.relevance: God's rule over the rise and fall of kingdoms.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The incarnation as the same God entering creation.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death… Therefore God has highly exalted him.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The hymn follows this arc: descent, death, exaltation, kingship.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: Ransomed… with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The sacrificial register verse three borrows.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The condition the hymn assumes but never states.

scriptureReferences.excerpt: On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.
scriptureReferences.relevance: The title the hymn drives toward and closes on.
